text:
The lighthouse at Carrow Point had stood for sixty years before Thomas Ashby came to keep it, and it would stand, he supposed, for sixty more after he was gone. He arrived on a grey morning in October with a single trunk and a letter from the Board, and the boatman who rowed him across the sound said nothing at all until the tower came into view above the rocks. Then he pointed with his chin and said that the last keeper had lasted eleven winters, which was thought to be a respectable number.

The tower was whitewashed on its seaward face and streaked with rust where the iron gallery met the stone. Inside, the stair wound up through three rooms, each smaller than the one below it, and the lamp room at the top was all glass and brass and the smell of paraffin. Ashby set down his trunk in the middle room and stood for a long while looking out at the water, which was the colour of pewter and moved in long slow folds toward the shore.

His duties were written on a card nailed beside the door. He was to trim the wicks at dusk and again at midnight, to wind the clockwork that turned the lens, to keep the log in ink and never in pencil, and to polish the glass every morning whether it seemed to need it or not. The card did not mention loneliness, and Ashby did not expect it to. He had been a clerk in a shipping office for nine years and had come to the coast precisely because he wanted a life in which the days were ruled by weather rather than by other men.

The first week passed in learning the sounds of the place. There was the wind, which came in from the west and pressed against the tower with a steady weight, and there was the sea below, which was never silent but was seldom loud. There were the gulls, who quarrelled on the ledges in the early morning, and there was the clockwork, whose ticking he could hear from every room once he had learned to listen for it. By the end of the week he found he could tell the hour from the light on the water without consulting the clock, and this pleased him more than he would have admitted to anyone.

Supplies came on the second Tuesday of each month, weather permitting, and the boatman brought with them whatever letters had accumulated at the post office in the village. Ashby had few correspondents. His sister wrote from the city with news of her children and her garden, and an old friend from the office sent him a newspaper now and then with the shipping columns marked in pencil. He read everything twice and then used the paper to light the stove.

In November the storms began in earnest. The first of them arrived in the night without any warning that Ashby could read, and he woke to find the whole tower humming like a struck bell. He climbed to the lamp room in his nightshirt and found the lens turning steadily, the flame upright and untroubled behind its glass, and he stood there until dawn watching the beam sweep out across a sea that seemed to be trying to climb the rocks. In the morning he wrote in the log that the light had burned without interruption, and he underlined the sentence, which was against the rules.

He learned to expect the storms after that, and to read the signs of them in the way the gulls left the ledges and the barometer in the middle room began its slow descent. He learned that the tower would hold, and that the noise of it holding was not the same as the noise of it failing, and that a man could sleep through a great deal once he had learned the difference. He learned to bake bread that was not entirely a disgrace and to mend his own stockings and to talk to himself in a low voice while he worked, so that the sound of speech did not go entirely out of his life.

By Christmas he had been alone for ten weeks, and he found, somewhat to his surprise, that he did not mind it. The boatman brought a small goose and a bottle of something dark and sweet, and Ashby cooked the goose badly and drank the bottle slowly and wrote a long letter to his sister in which he tried to explain why he was content. He did not think he succeeded, but he sent the letter anyway, and he stood on the gallery in the cold to watch the boat carry it back across the sound toward the lamps of the village, which came on one by one as the dark came down.

When old Master Penhallow took on an apprentice, the town of Weybridge agreed that it was about time, for the clockmaker was past seventy and his hands had begun to shake in the mornings. The boy he chose was Daniel Rowe, the son of a widow who kept a lodging house by the mill, and the arrangement was that Daniel should sleep above the shop, eat at the master's table, and learn whatever the master saw fit to teach him over a term of seven years.

The shop stood at the corner of Bridge Street and the market square, and its window held a single tall clock in a walnut case that had not been for sale in living memory. Inside there were clocks on every wall and on most of the shelves, and their ticking made a sound like rain on a slate roof. Daniel, who had grown up in a house full of lodgers and noise, found that he could not sleep the first night for the ticking, and then found on the second night that he could not sleep without it.

Master Penhallow was not a talkative man. He taught by doing a thing once, slowly, and then handing over the tools and watching. In the first month Daniel learned to clean a movement without losing any of its parts, which was harder than it sounded, and to file a pivot true, and to tell by ear whether an escapement was beating evenly. He learned that a clock which ran fast was not a clock which had too much energy but a clock whose pendulum was too short, and that most faults in the trade were faults of proportion rather than of force.

The master had one rule that he repeated more often than any other, which was that a clock must never be made to seem to work. It must work, or it must be taken apart until the reason it did not work had been found. Daniel had at first thought this a needlessly severe way to put a plain idea, but he came to see that there were a hundred ways of making a clock seem to work, and that most of them were quicker than the one true way, and that the temptation to take them was strongest exactly when a customer was waiting.

In the spring of his second year a farmer from the hills brought in a long-case clock that had belonged to his grandmother. It had stopped, he said, on the night she died, and had not been persuaded to go since, and he wanted it going again by the time his daughter was married in June. Master Penhallow looked at the movement for a long while and then handed it to Daniel and went to sit by the stove, which was his way of saying that the job was the apprentice's to do or to fail at.

Daniel took the movement apart over three days and laid every piece out on a cloth in the order in which it had come free. He found nothing broken. The springs were sound, the wheels were true, the pivots were worn but not badly, and the escapement, when he set it up alone on the bench, beat as evenly as anything in the shop. He put it all back together and it ran for six hours and stopped. He took it apart again. On the fourth day he found the fault, which was a hair of brass no longer than an eyelash, wedged where the great wheel met the plate, and which caught only when the wheel had turned to one particular tooth.

He showed it to the master on the tip of a needle, and the old man looked at it for some time and then nodded once and went back to the stove. The clock was delivered in May, and the farmer paid in coin and in a ham, and Daniel was allowed to keep the ham, which he took home to his mother's lodging house, where it lasted a fortnight and was much discussed.

The years went by in that fashion. Daniel grew taller and the master grew smaller, and the ticking in the shop went on as it had always done. There came a winter when the master's hands would no longer hold a file at all, and he sat by the stove through the whole of it, watching, and saying less than ever. In the spring he told Daniel that the tall clock in the window was his now, and that it had never been for sale because it was the first clock the master had ever made, and that it had a fault in the striking train that he had never been able to find. Daniel found it in a week. He did not tell the old man, and the clock stayed in the window, and it was there still when Daniel had apprentices of his own.

We left the inn at Stanbury a little after seven, when the mist was still lying in the bottom of the valley like milk in a bowl, and took the cart road that follows the river up toward the high pastures. There were four of us, with two ponies for the baggage, and a guide named Hollis who had been recommended to us by the innkeeper as a man who knew every stone between the village and the pass. He walked ahead with his hands behind his back and did not speak unless a question was put to him, and then he answered it fully and stopped.

The river for the first three miles is broad and slow and the colour of strong tea, and the road keeps company with it closely, so that one hears the water all morning without often seeing it through the alders. Then the valley narrows and the road climbs and the river drops away below into a gorge, and the sound of it changes from a murmur to a steady roar that one feels in the chest before one hears it. Hollis told us that the gorge was called the Throat and that a mill had once stood at the head of it, though nothing remained of the mill but a line of dressed stones in the grass.

We stopped for bread and cheese at a place where the road crosses the river by a bridge of a single arch. The bridge is old and narrow and has no parapet, and the ponies did not like it, and there was some difficulty in getting them across. From the middle of the arch one can look straight down into the water, which is very clear at that point and runs over stones of a pale green colour that Hollis said were prized by the people of the valley for their grinding qualities.

Above the bridge the character of the country alters entirely. The alders give way to birch and then to nothing but grass and stone, and the valley opens out into a broad shallow basin ringed with hills that seem near and are not. The light is different up there. It falls from a wider sky and it lies on the grass in a way that makes the whole basin seem to be gently shining, and we all four fell silent for a time as we walked into it, though none of us could have said afterward exactly what had silenced us.

There are sheep in the basin in summer, and the shepherds live in stone huts that are roofed with turf and have no windows. We passed two of these huts and found them empty, with the ash cold in the hearth and a bundle of dry heather laid ready for the next man to come. Hollis said that this was the custom of the valley and that a man who used a hut and did not leave it ready would be known of within a week, though he could not explain how the knowledge would travel.

The pass itself is not dramatic. The road simply goes on climbing until it stops climbing, and one finds oneself standing on a saddle of short grass with the basin behind and another valley opening ahead, greener and more wooded, with the roofs of a village visible far down at its mouth. There is a cairn on the saddle to which every traveller adds a stone, and we added ours, and Hollis added his without any sign that he had done it a hundred times before.

We ate our supper in the lee of the cairn and watched the light go off the hills one after another, the highest last. Hollis pointed out the peaks by name and told us which of them could be climbed and which could not and which had been climbed by people who ought to have known better. He had been up most of them himself. When the last of the light had gone we went down into the far valley by lantern, which took three hours and was the hardest part of the day, and we reached the village with the ponies stumbling and ourselves very tired and entirely content.

I set this down not because the journey was remarkable in itself, for it is one that the people of the valley make in both directions every week of the summer, but because I have found that I think of the basin more often than I think of a good many places that were harder to reach. There is something in a wide shallow place with a wide sky over it that stays in the mind, and I should like to go back there before I am too old to manage the bridge.

We consider the numerical solution of banded linear systems whose coefficients vary slowly along the diagonal, a structure that arises in the discretisation of one-dimensional boundary value problems with smoothly varying material properties. The standard direct method for such systems is banded Gaussian elimination, which costs a number of operations proportional to the product of the system size and the square of the bandwidth. For narrow bands this cost is modest, and the method is stable whenever the matrix is diagonally dominant. Our interest is in the regime where the band is moderately wide and the dominance is weak, so that pivoting cannot be avoided and the fill-in it produces begins to erode the advantage of the banded structure.

The iterative alternative we study is a block relaxation scheme in which the system is partitioned into overlapping windows of a fixed width and each window is solved exactly in turn, with the overlap region providing the coupling between successive solves. Schemes of this kind have been proposed many times under different names, and the question of when they converge is well understood in the symmetric positive definite case. The nonsymmetric case is less settled, and the smooth variation of the coefficients suggests that a local analysis should be possible.

Our main result is an estimate for the contraction factor of one sweep in terms of two quantities: the ratio of the window width to the bandwidth, and a measure of the rate at which the coefficients vary across a window. When the coefficients are constant the estimate reduces to a known bound for the block Jacobi iteration. When they vary, the estimate degrades by a term proportional to the variation, and we show by example that this degradation is not an artefact of the proof. The examples are constructed by taking a constant coefficient system for which the iteration converges and perturbing the coefficients by a slowly varying function of controlled amplitude.

The proof proceeds by writing the error after one sweep as the product of window-local error propagators and bounding each factor in a weighted norm whose weight is chosen to match the local coefficient values. The weight is where the smoothness assumption enters: it must change slowly enough across a window that the norm inequalities for adjacent windows can be chained together. We give the argument in detail for the case of two overlapping windows and then indicate how it extends to any number.

We also report numerical experiments on three families of test problems. The first family is a convection diffusion equation on an interval with a coefficient that varies sinusoidally, the second is a fourth-order beam equation with a stepwise varying stiffness, and the third is a set of matrices with randomly generated smooth coefficients whose variation rate can be dialled continuously. In every case the observed contraction factor is within a small constant of the estimate, and in the third family the dependence on the variation rate matches the estimate closely across two orders of magnitude.

A practical consequence of the analysis is a rule for choosing the window width. Wider windows converge faster per sweep but cost more per sweep, and the estimate makes the tradeoff explicit enough that the optimum can be located without trial. For the sinusoidal test problem the predicted optimum is within one window width of the observed optimum at every problem size we tried. We do not claim that the rule is sharp in general, only that it is a reasonable default in the absence of other information.

Several questions remain open. The estimate requires that the coefficients vary smoothly in an absolute sense, and it would be more useful to have a version that tolerates isolated jumps, since these occur in most applications. The extension to two spatial dimensions, where the windows become blocks and the overlap becomes a strip, is straightforward to state but we have not carried out the analysis. Finally, the relationship between the contraction factor of the relaxation scheme and the conditioning of the preconditioned system that it defines, when used as a preconditioner for a Krylov method, deserves a separate treatment.

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section two sets out the notation and the assumptions on the coefficient functions. Section three states the main estimate and gives the proof for two windows. Section four extends the proof to many windows and discusses the constants. Section five presents the numerical experiments, and section six concludes with the open questions listed above and some remarks on the parallel implementation of the scheme, which is natural because the window solves within a sweep are independent apart from the overlap exchange.

This note concerns the problem of estimating, online, the effective rank of a matrix whose columns arrive one at a time and whose column space drifts slowly with the index. The setting is motivated by streaming signal processing applications in which the observations are high-dimensional vectors that lie near a low-dimensional subspace, and the subspace rotates gradually over the course of the stream. A tracker that maintains an orthonormal basis for the subspace must decide how many basis vectors to keep, and the decision must be made from the data alone without a second pass.

The naive approach is to maintain a running estimate of the covariance and to count its eigenvalues above a threshold. This is exact in the stationary case and fails in the drifting case because the covariance averages over the whole history, so that a subspace which has rotated out of the current column space continues to contribute eigenvalues long after it has ceased to be relevant. Forgetting factors mitigate the problem at the cost of introducing a parameter that must be tuned to the unknown drift rate, and a mistuned factor either lags the drift or inflates the rank with noise.

We propose instead to estimate the rank from the residual of a fixed-rank projection. If the tracker keeps a basis of dimension r and projects each incoming column onto it, the norm of the residual is small when r is at least the true rank and large when it is less. The sequence of residual norms therefore carries information about whether r should be increased, and a simple test on that sequence suffices to decide. The test we use compares the mean residual over a short window to the noise level, which is itself estimated from the residuals of the least significant retained direction.

The decision to decrease r is harder, because a direction that has rotated out of the column space does not announce itself through the residual, which is already small. We handle this by tracking the energy captured by each retained direction over the same short window and dropping a direction whose captured energy falls below the noise level for a fixed number of consecutive windows. The number of windows is the only parameter of the scheme, and we show that the scheme is insensitive to it over a range of an order of magnitude.

Our analysis treats the case in which the true subspace rotates at a constant angular rate and the noise is isotropic. Under these assumptions we show that the residual test increases r within a delay proportional to the window length once a new direction enters, and that the energy test decreases r within a delay proportional to the product of the window length and the number of confirmation windows once an old direction leaves. Both delays are independent of the ambient dimension, which is the property that makes the scheme practical for high-dimensional streams.

The analysis also identifies a failure mode. If the rotation rate is fast enough that a direction enters and leaves within a single window, the residual test and the energy test can disagree, and the rank estimate oscillates. We characterise the rate at which this happens in terms of the window length and show that it can be avoided by choosing the window shorter than the inverse rotation rate, which is a condition the user can check when the rotation rate is known and can estimate from the oscillation itself when it is not.

Experiments on synthetic streams confirm the analysis and on two real data sets, a set of sensor readings from a structural monitoring array and a set of frames from a fixed surveillance camera, the scheme tracks the rank changes produced by known events with delays that match the predicted ones. In the camera data the rank increases when a vehicle enters the scene and decreases when it leaves, and the delays are within a factor of two of the predictions despite the noise being neither isotropic nor stationary.

We close with a remark on the relation between this scheme and the family of incremental singular value decomposition algorithms, which also maintain a basis and also face the rank selection problem. Those algorithms typically truncate to a fixed rank after each update, and our residual and energy tests can be attached to any of them at negligible cost, since the residual is computed in the course of the update and the captured energies are the squared singular values. We have done this for one such algorithm and found that the combined method behaves as the analysis predicts, but a systematic comparison across the family is beyond the scope of this note.

We report measurements of suspended sediment concentration in a small gravel-bed river over the course of a single spring flood, together with a simple model that reproduces the main features of the record. The river drains a catchment of about forty square kilometres of mixed pasture and woodland, and the reach we instrumented is a straight section of two hundred metres with a stable bank on one side and a gently eroding bank on the other. The instrumentation consisted of a pressure transducer for stage, an optical backscatter sensor for turbidity, and an automatic pump sampler that drew a bottle every hour during the rising limb and every three hours during the recession.

The flood was produced by three days of steady rain on ground that was already near saturation, and the stage rose from its base level to a peak of just under two metres over thirty hours before receding over the following six days. The turbidity record shows the familiar clockwise hysteresis in which concentrations on the rising limb exceed those on the falling limb at the same stage, and the pump samples, which were filtered and weighed in the laboratory, confirm the turbidity record to within the scatter expected from the sensor calibration.

The hysteresis is usually attributed to the exhaustion of a finite store of readily mobilised fine material on the bed and banks. Early in the flood this store is depleted rapidly, producing high concentrations, and later in the flood the supply is limited to what is delivered from the catchment, which lags the stage. We tested this explanation by walking the reach after the flood and mapping the sources of fine material, and we found that the eroding bank had retreated by up to half a metre along a stretch of thirty metres, which is consistent in volume with the total sediment yield estimated from the record.

The model we fitted treats the store as a single reservoir that is emptied at a rate proportional to the product of its contents and the excess of the stage above a threshold, and refilled at a constant rate representing catchment delivery. This is a two-parameter model once the threshold is fixed from the record, and it reproduces the timing of the concentration peak, the ratio of rising to falling limb concentrations, and the shape of the recession, with residuals that are comparable to the sampling scatter. It does not reproduce a secondary peak on the second day, which we attribute to a bank collapse observed in the field and not to the river.

We compared the fitted parameters with those reported for similar reaches in the literature and found the emptying rate to be at the high end of the reported range, which we attribute to the unusually erodible bank material at our site. The refilling rate is close to the median. We also examined the sensitivity of the fit to the choice of threshold and found that the model is robust to changes of a few centimetres, which is the precision with which the threshold can be read from the record in any case.

The main limitation of the study is its scale. One flood in one reach is a case, not a sample, and the agreement between the model and the record may reflect the flexibility of a two-parameter fit as much as the correctness of the reservoir description. We have tried to guard against this by fixing the threshold independently and by checking the volume balance against the field survey, but a proper test would require several floods, ideally of different sizes, on the same reach. The instrumentation is still in place and we intend to report on subsequent events.

A second limitation is that the optical sensor responds to particle size as well as to concentration, and the pump samples suggest that the size distribution coarsened over the flood. We have not attempted to correct for this, and the concentrations reported on the falling limb may therefore be slight underestimates. The effect is in the direction that would reduce the apparent hysteresis, so our conclusion about its magnitude is conservative.

The data set, the calibration curves, and the model code are available from the authors on request. We have deposited the raw turbidity and stage records with the regional hydrological archive under the reach identifier given in the appendix, and we encourage anyone with comparable records from other reaches to compare them with the model, which is simple enough to be fitted by hand to a plotted record in an afternoon.

Marrow Bridge is a stone arch bridge crossing the River Tayle at the town of Ashcombe in the fictional county of Wessling. Completed in 1784 to a design attributed to the county surveyor Edmund Halloway, it replaced a timber crossing that had been damaged repeatedly by winter floods. The bridge has five semicircular arches of dressed limestone, with cutwaters on the upstream side and a parapet of coped ashlar. It carries a single carriageway and two footways and remains in daily use, although heavy vehicles have been prohibited since 1962.

The earliest recorded crossing at the site was a ford, mentioned in a manorial survey of 1312 as the point at which the road from Ashcombe to the coast met the river. A timber bridge is first recorded in 1451, when the town accounts note a payment for its repair. This bridge, or a series of replacements on the same alignment, served the town for more than three centuries. The accounts record major repairs in 1533, 1601, 1655 and 1722, and the surviving minutes of the town council describe the structure in 1770 as being in a dangerous condition.

In 1779 the council petitioned the county for a stone bridge, citing the cost of the repeated repairs and the interruption to trade whenever the timber bridge was closed. The petition was granted in 1781 and construction began the following spring. Halloway's design was conservative for its date, using semicircular rather than segmental arches, which required taller piers but was thought to be more robust against scour. The stone was quarried at Ferring Down, about six miles to the north, and brought to the site by cart. The bridge was opened in October 1784 with a procession and a dinner for the workmen, the cost of which is recorded in the council accounts.

The bridge has been altered twice. In 1841 the parapet was raised by about thirty centimetres following a fatal accident, and the original coping stones were reused on top of a new course of ashlar. In 1897 the carriageway was widened by corbelling out the footways on cast iron brackets, an arrangement that survives on the downstream side. The upstream footway was returned to its original width in 1988 when the brackets were found to be corroded, and the bridge was closed for four months while the work was carried out.

Marrow Bridge was designated a listed structure in 1954, and the listing text describes it as a well-preserved example of a late eighteenth century county bridge with unusually complete documentation. The council accounts, petition and construction records are held at the county archive, and a set of Halloway's drawings, showing the arch centring and the foundation piling, was discovered in a solicitor's office in 1971 and is now displayed in the town museum.

The bridge features in the local tradition that the arches were designed to be exactly the width of a loaded hay wagon, so that any wagon that could pass under one arch could pass under all five, and that a wagon which stuck under the middle arch during the opening procession was found to have been overloaded by the driver in expectation of a larger crowd. The story is not supported by the accounts, which record no such incident, but it is repeated on an information board at the western end of the bridge.

The river at the bridge is tidal at spring tides, and the piers show a distinct band of weathering at the level of the highest tides. Salmon were recorded passing under the bridge until the 1930s, and a fish pass was installed on the weir upstream in 2009 in an attempt to restore the run. The bridge is a popular viewpoint for the annual raft race, which starts from the weir and finishes at the quay below the town.

An annual inspection of the structure is carried out by the county highways authority, and the most recent published report describes the arches as sound and the cutwaters as showing minor loss of pointing. The bridge is included in a proposed conservation area covering the riverside part of the town, on which consultation began in 2021, and a management plan for the structure was adopted by the town council in the same year.

Halden Observatory is an astronomical observatory located on Halden Fell, a hill of about six hundred metres above sea level in the fictional northern district of Corrow. Founded in 1878 by the industrialist and amateur astronomer Josiah Brant, it was one of the first observatories in the region to be sited at altitude specifically to escape the smoke of the nearby manufacturing towns. The observatory is now operated by the regional university and is used for teaching, for a long-running programme of variable star observation, and for public open evenings during the winter months.

Brant made his fortune in the manufacture of textile machinery and took up astronomy in middle age after attending a public lecture on the transit of Venus. He purchased the summit of Halden Fell in 1876, built a road to it at his own expense, and commissioned a telescope of thirty centimetres aperture from a maker in the capital. The instrument was housed in a dome of his own design, which rotated on cannon balls set in a circular channel, an arrangement that proved troublesome in frost and was replaced by a conventional wheeled ring in 1902.

Brant used the observatory for double star measurement, and his catalogue of two thousand pairs, published in 1891, remained a standard reference for several decades. He also began the programme of variable star observation that continues today, recording the brightness of a set of long-period variables by eye against comparison stars on every clear night. His observing books, which run to forty volumes, are held in the university library and have been digitised.

After Brant's death in 1908 the observatory passed to a trust that he had established, and it was operated by a succession of resident astronomers until 1949, when the trust's funds were exhausted and the site was transferred to the university. The university added a second dome in 1956 to house a forty centimetre reflector, and a third in 1994 for a robotic instrument that operates without an observer present. The original Brant telescope remains in use for public evenings and is maintained in its original mounting.

The observing conditions at Halden Fell are good for the region but poor by international standards. The site enjoys about one hundred and twenty clear nights a year, and the sky brightness has increased steadily since the 1960s with the growth of the towns to the south. A local lighting ordinance introduced in 2004 halted the increase in the northern half of the sky, and measurements made by the observatory have been used to support similar ordinances elsewhere.

The variable star programme is the observatory's principal scientific contribution. The set of stars established by Brant has been observed continuously for more than a century, with the visual method replaced by photographic measurement in the 1930s and by electronic detectors in the 1980s, and the resulting record is one of the longest homogeneous brightness series in existence for several of the stars. The record has been used to detect slow changes in the periods of long-period variables and to identify a small number of stars whose behaviour changed abruptly during the twentieth century.

The observatory holds public open evenings on Friday nights between October and March, at which visitors may look through the Brant telescope and attend a short talk. The evenings are popular and are usually fully booked several weeks in advance. A small museum in the original meridian room displays Brant's instruments, a selection of his observing books, and a working model of the cannon ball dome mechanism.

Access to the site is by the road that Brant built, which is single track with passing places and is closed in snow. The university operates a minibus from the town railway station on open evenings. The buildings were listed in 1987, and the listing text notes the cannon ball channel, which survives beneath the modern ring, as a rare example of a nineteenth century dome bearing.

The Orrin dialect is a variety of the fictional Vessic language spoken in the Orrin valley and the adjacent coastal strip in the north of the country. It is distinguished from the standard language by a number of phonological features, most notably the retention of a distinction between long and short vowels that has been lost elsewhere, and by a vocabulary that preserves a number of terms relating to fishing, salt production and upland pasture that are obsolete or unknown in other varieties. The dialect has about thirty thousand speakers, most of them over the age of fifty, and is classified as vulnerable.

The valley was relatively isolated until the construction of the coast road in the 1920s, and the dialect developed with little influence from the standard language during the period in which the standard was being fixed by printing and schooling. Early descriptions of the dialect were made by clergymen in the eighteenth century, who noted the vowel length distinction and recorded word lists, and a systematic survey was carried out in the 1890s by the philologist Ansel Marrick, whose grammar and glossary remain the principal reference.

The vowel length distinction operates in stressed syllables and is contrastive in a number of minimal pairs, some of which are used by speakers of the standard language to identify Orrin speakers. In addition to length, the dialect has a rounded front vowel that has merged with the corresponding unrounded vowel in the standard, and a set of falling diphthongs that the standard has simplified to long vowels. The consonant system is close to the standard, with the exception of a voiceless lateral that occurs word-initially in a small number of words.

The grammar of the dialect differs from the standard mainly in the verb, which retains a distinct plural form in the past tense and a separate form for the second person singular that the standard uses only in liturgical contexts. Word order is somewhat freer than in the standard, particularly in questions, where the verb may precede or follow the subject with a difference in emphasis rather than in meaning. The dialect also has a number of particles used to mark the speaker's attitude to a statement, several of which have no equivalent in the standard.

The vocabulary preserves a number of terms that Marrick considered to be survivals from an earlier stage of the language. These include a set of words for the different states of the tide, a set for the different kinds of salt produced by evaporation, and a set for the ages and conditions of sheep, of which he recorded more than forty. Many of these terms have fallen out of use with the decline of the industries to which they belonged, and a survey in 2015 found that fewer than a fifth of the tidal terms were known to speakers under forty.

The dialect has a small written literature, consisting mainly of verse published in local newspapers in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries and of a number of collections of stories recorded from speakers in the 1950s and 1960s. There is no standard orthography, and writers have generally adapted the standard spelling with additional marks for vowel length. A proposal for a standard orthography was published in 2008 and has been adopted by the regional council for signage but is not widely used otherwise.

Attitudes to the dialect have changed over the past century. It was discouraged in schools until the 1970s and was widely regarded by its own speakers as a marker of rural backwardness. Since the 1980s it has been promoted by the regional council and by a voluntary association as a part of the local heritage, and it is now taught as an option in the valley's secondary schools. The number of speakers continues to fall, but the rate of decline has slowed, and a small number of younger speakers have acquired the dialect as a second variety.

Recordings of the dialect made between 1952 and 1968 are held by the national sound archive and have been made available online. A dictionary based on Marrick's glossary and on the recordings was published in 2019 and is the most complete description of the vocabulary. A grammar intended for learners was published in 2021 by the voluntary association and is used in the school courses.

I have kept a notebook for most of my adult life, and for most of that time I have been slightly embarrassed about it. Not about the keeping, which seems harmless enough, but about the contents, which are not what a notebook is supposed to contain. There are no great thoughts in mine. There are lists of things to do, most of them done long ago, and half-sentences that meant something once, and the occasional drawing of a chair. If someone found it after I was gone they would learn nothing about me except that I was often in rooms with chairs.

And yet I would not give it up, and I have come to think that the reason has nothing to do with what the notebook holds and everything to do with what the act of writing in it does to the day. A day in which I have written something down, however trivial, has a shape. It has a moment in it when I stopped and looked at what was happening and decided it was worth a line. A day without that moment is not worse, exactly, but it is smoother, and smooth days slide past without leaving anything to hold on to.

People who do not keep notebooks sometimes ask what the point is if you never read them back, and it is true that I almost never do. I have tried, and the experience is not pleasant. The old entries are either boring or faintly painful, and the ones that are neither are the ones I remember anyway. But the question assumes that the notebook is a storage device, and I do not think it is. It is closer to a musical instrument. Nobody asks a pianist what the point is if the music does not stay in the room.

The best notebooks I have seen belonged to people who used them for work of some kind, and the work gave the notebook a spine. A naturalist's notebook has dates and places and weather in it because those things matter to the observations, and the observations are what the notebook is for. A programmer's notebook has diagrams in it that nobody else could read. A cook's has quantities crossed out and rewritten. The notebook takes its shape from the work, and the work is improved by having somewhere to be thought about that is not the place where it gets done.

I think the reason my own notebook is so shapeless is that I have never quite decided what my work is, and so the notebook has had to make do with whatever came along. This sounds like a complaint, and it is partly one, but there is also something to be said for a notebook that is not in service to anything. It is the one place where I am not trying to be useful. The lists are useful, I suppose, but the drawings of chairs are not, and I have noticed that the drawings are the entries I am least embarrassed by, which suggests that usefulness was never really the point.

There is a practical argument for notebooks that I should mention, which is that writing something down is the most reliable way I know of finding out whether you actually think it. A great many opinions survive in the mind only because they have never been asked to stand up on a page. When you write them down they either stand or they do not, and if they do not, you have learned something at the cost of a few lines of ink. This is a cheap price for a genuine discovery, and it is a discovery that no amount of thinking will produce, because thinking is exactly the process that lets the weak opinions hide.

I do not want to overstate the case. A notebook is a small thing, and the world is full of people who do fine without one. But I have noticed that the people I most admire tend to have some equivalent, whether it is a notebook or a sketchbook or a habit of writing long letters, and I do not think this is an accident. They have somewhere to put the things that do not fit yet, and having somewhere to put them is what makes it possible to notice them in the first place.

So I will go on keeping mine, and go on being slightly embarrassed about it, and go on drawing chairs. If there is a lesson here it is only that the value of a habit is not always in what it produces, and that a thing which produces nothing can still be worth doing, provided it changes the shape of the day.

There is a kind of tool that lasts, and it is not the kind you would expect. The tools that last are not the most powerful or the most complete. They are the ones that do one thing in a way that is easy to understand and hard to get wrong, and that leave enough undone that they can be combined with other tools to do the things they do not do themselves. I have been trying for some years to work out why this should be, and I think I have at least part of an answer.

The obvious explanation is that small tools are easier to maintain, and there is something in this. A tool that does one thing has a smaller surface to keep working, and when the world changes around it there is less that needs to change with it. But this cannot be the whole story, because plenty of small tools have been abandoned, and some very large ones have lasted for decades. The size of a tool is a poor predictor of its lifespan on its own.

A better explanation, I think, is that small tools are easier to trust. When you use a tool that does one thing, you can hold the whole of what it does in your head, and so when it does something unexpected you know immediately that the unexpected thing came from somewhere else. A large tool cannot be held in the head, and so when it does something unexpected you do not know whether the tool is wrong or you are, and the only way to find out is to read the manual, and nobody reads the manual. Over time, the small tool accumulates trust and the large tool accumulates suspicion, and trust is what keeps a tool in use.

There is a related point about composition. A tool that does one thing can be combined with other tools that do one thing, and the combinations can do things that nobody planned. A large tool that does many things can only be combined with itself, because its parts were designed to fit each other and not to fit anything else. So the small tool has a larger space of possible uses than the large one, even though the large one does more on its own, and a tool with more possible uses is a tool that more people will find a reason to keep.

None of this means that large tools are a mistake. There are jobs that need them, and there are people who need the job done more than they need to understand how. But it does mean that when you are building a tool and you are not sure whether to make it do one more thing, the answer is usually no. The one more thing will make the tool more useful to the person who asked for it and less trustworthy to everyone else, and everyone else is where the tool's future lies.

I want to say something about a particular temptation, which is the temptation to make a tool complete. A complete tool is one that anticipates every need and provides for it, so that the user never has to reach for anything else. This sounds like a virtue and is nearly always a vice, because the needs that were anticipated are the needs the builder had, and the users have different ones. The complete tool ends up being complete for one person and awkward for everybody, and the awkwardness is permanent, because completeness cannot be taken away without breaking someone.

The tools I use most are all incomplete in ways that I have stopped noticing. They do the thing I need and stop, and when I need something else I use something else. It took me a long time to see that this was a design decision rather than a limitation, and longer still to see that it was the right one. The builders of those tools resisted the temptation to be complete, and their restraint is the reason I am still using what they built.

If I had to compress all this into a rule, it would be that a tool should be small enough to understand, sharp enough to be worth understanding, and open enough to be combined with things its builder never heard of. That is three rules, not one, but they pull in the same direction, and a tool that follows all three has a good chance of outlasting the people who made it.

Most of the useful ideas I have had came to me while walking, and I have long suspected that this is not a coincidence. Walking has some property that makes it good for thinking, and I have spent a fair amount of time, much of it while walking, trying to work out what the property is. I do not have a complete answer, but I have some partial ones, and they seem worth setting down.

The first thing to say is that walking is not the same as exercise. Running does not produce ideas, at least not for me, and neither does anything that requires attention to the body. Walking is slow enough and familiar enough that the body can be left to manage itself, and the mind is set free without being set entirely adrift. There is a rhythm to it that seems to matter, though I could not tell you why a rhythm should help, and the rhythm is one that you do not have to think about, which may be the point.

The second thing is that walking takes you past things. A mind that is trying to think about a problem tends to go around and around in the same small space, and the things it needs are often outside that space. When you walk, the world keeps presenting you with things you were not looking for, and every so often one of them turns out to be the thing you needed. This does not happen at a desk, where the world is arranged to present you with only the things you were looking for, which are by definition the things you already have.

The third thing, and I think the most important, is that walking makes it impossible to write anything down. This sounds like a disadvantage and is in fact the reverse. When you can write things down, you do, and writing a thing down is a way of stopping thinking about it. The idea goes onto the page and the mind moves on. When you cannot write things down, the idea has to be held, and holding it means turning it over, and turning it over is where the work gets done. By the time you get home the idea has usually either fallen apart or become something better than what you started with, and both outcomes are useful.

I have noticed that the length of the walk matters, and that the useful length is longer than seems reasonable. The first twenty minutes are spent shedding whatever you were doing before, and nothing much happens in them. The ideas, if they are going to come, come after that, and they keep coming for as long as you keep walking, which is why I have come to think of a walk of less than an hour as a warm-up rather than a walk.

The route matters less than I would have guessed. I used to think that new places would produce more ideas than familiar ones, on the grounds that there would be more to notice, and there is something in this, but the effect is smaller than the effect of simply being out and moving. A walk I have done a hundred times will still produce ideas, and there is even an argument that the familiar route is better, because the noticing takes less attention and there is more left over for the problem.

I should say that walking does not produce ideas out of nothing. It produces them out of whatever you have been putting into your head in the days before, and if you have been putting nothing in, you will get nothing out. The walk is where the sorting happens, not the gathering. This is obvious when stated but easy to forget, and I have gone on a good many walks in the hope of an idea when what I actually needed was to read something first.

I am aware that all this is anecdote, and that there are people who think best in the bath or on trains or at four in the morning, and I have no argument with them. But I do think that anyone who has to think for a living should find out where their thinking happens, and should arrange to be there more often, and should be a little suspicious of the assumption that the place is a desk. For me it is a path, and I have stopped apologising for the amount of time I spend on it.
